options.A: A rough guide calling for investigation of significant departures, and not as an absolute rule that every enterprise must meet regardless of its size, age and circumstances
options.B: A target which the enterprise must attain in the following year in all cases
options.C: A substitute for examining the enterprise's own trend over time
options.D: A figure which proves mismanagement whenever the enterprise falls below it

q: Altman's Z-score model is used in financial statement analysis primarily to:

options.A: Compute the cost of capital of an enterprise
options.B: Fix the optimum dividend policy of a company
options.C: Work out the break-even point of a firm
options.D: Assess the likelihood of an enterprise failing (going bankrupt) by combining several financial ratios into a single discriminant score

q: In Altman's Z-score model, the first variable, X1, is the ratio of working capital to total assets. An enterprise has working capital of Rs 3,00,000 and total assets of Rs 15,00,000. The value of X1 is:
An enterprise has an Altman Z-score of 1.5. On the conventional interpretation of the model, the enterprise falls in:

options.A: The safe zone, with negligible risk of failure
options.B: The distress zone, since the score is below 1.81
options.C: The grey zone, since the score lies between 1.81 and 2.99
options.D: A zone which the model does not recognise

q: The original Altman Z-score model combines:

options.A: Five financial ratios, covering working capital position, retained earnings, operating earnings, the market value of equity against liabilities, and sales generation from assets
options.B: Only the current ratio and the debt-equity ratio
options.C: Only profitability ratios drawn from the profit and loss account
options.D: Cash-flow ratios exclusively

q: A recognised limitation of applying Altman's Z-score, in its original form, to an enterprise today is that:

options.A: The model uses too few ratios to be of any use
options.B: The score can be computed only for government companies
options.C: The model requires the enterprise to have failed once already
options.D: The model was developed from a sample of manufacturing companies of a particular country and period, so that its weights and cut-off scores may not hold unchanged for other industries, countries or periods

q: An enterprise has net cash flow from operating activities of Rs 9,60,000 and current liabilities of Rs 4,00,000. Its operating cash flow ratio is:

An enterprise has net cash flow from operating activities of Rs 5,40,000. During the year it paid interest of Rs 1,20,000 and income tax of Rs 60,000, both of which were charged in arriving at the operating cash flow. Its cash interest coverage, computed as (operating cash flow + interest paid + tax paid) divided by interest paid, is:

options.A: 4.5 times
options.B: 6 times
options.C: 7.2 times
options.D: 5 times

q: The ratio of cash flow from operating activities to capital expenditure works out to more than 1 for an enterprise. This indicates that:

options.A: The enterprise has generated enough cash from its operations to meet its capital expenditure for the year without depending on outside financing for that purpose
options.B: The enterprise has necessarily earned a profit for the year
options.C: The enterprise has no long-term borrowings outstanding
options.D: The capital expenditure of the enterprise was wrongly recorded

q: An enterprise reports cash flow from operating activities of Rs 14,00,000 and capital expenditure of Rs 9,00,000 during a year. Its free cash flow for the year is:

Over three successive years, the reported profit after tax of an enterprise rises steadily, but its cash flow from operating activities steadily falls. For an analyst judging the quality of the reported earnings, this pattern is a warning sign principally because:

options.A: Profits and operating cash flow must always move together by law
options.B: A rising profit should always be accompanied by a rising dividend
options.C: Profits increasingly unsupported by operating cash suggest that earnings rest heavily on accruals, such as swelling debtors or stocks, rather than on cash actually realised
options.D: The enterprise must have changed its financial year

q: Earnings of an enterprise are regarded as being of high quality when they:

options.A: Are the highest ever reported by the enterprise
options.B: Arise mainly from gains on the sale of fixed assets and investments
options.C: Fluctuate widely from year to year without explanation
options.D: Are persistent in nature, arise from the recurring operations of the enterprise and are backed by corresponding operating cash flows

q: Which of the following practices amounts to 'window dressing' of the balance sheet?

options.A: Cheques drawn in favour of creditors are entered in the books before the close of the year but are actually despatched only after the year-end, so that the balances shown at that date do not represent the true position
options.B: Depreciation is charged on plant at the rate consistently followed in earlier years
options.C: A provision for doubtful debts is created on a prudent estimate
options.D: Stock is valued at cost or net realisable value, whichever is lower

q: An analyst who suspects window dressing in the year-end balance sheet of an enterprise can best protect his conclusions by:

options.A: Relying exclusively on the year-end balance sheet itself
options.B: Ignoring the cash flow statement for the year
options.C: Discarding all ratios computed from balance sheet figures
options.D: Using average balances for the year in place of year-end balances alone, and examining transactions entered into immediately before and after the balance sheet date

q: Without any change in its operations or cash position, an enterprise raises its reported profit for the year substantially by lengthening the estimated useful life of its plant, thereby reducing the depreciation charge. For earnings-quality analysis, this change is significant because:

options.A: It proves that the plant will actually last longer
options.B: It increases the operating cash flow of the enterprise by the same amount
options.C: The higher profit rests on a change in an accounting estimate rather than on improved performance, and the lower charge will not recur in the same way once asset replacements fall due
options.D: It reduces the tax payable by the enterprise to nil

q: An enterprise reports profit after tax of Rs 7,20,000 and cash flow from operating activities of Rs 5,40,000. Its average total assets are Rs 36,00,000. The accrual component of its earnings, measured as (profit after tax minus operating cash flow) divided by average total assets, is:

options.A: 2 per cent
options.B: 5 per cent
options.C: 15 per cent
options.D: 20 per cent
